title: Be to + infinitive; be about to + infinitive
subtitle: are to visit / are about to eat
summary: Use be to + infinitive for official or planned future events that people can control, and be about to + infinitive for something happening in the very near future.

lesson.heading: News reports: be to + infinitive
lesson.text: Be to + infinitive is very common in news reports to talk about events that are likely to happen in the near future. The passive form is often used.

examples.text: Police officers **are to visit** every home in the area.
The main Rome-to-Naples railway line **is to be reopened** today.

lesson.heading: Official arrangements, instructions and orders
lesson.text: We also use be to + infinitive for formal or official arrangements, for formal instructions and to give orders. Passive forms make an order or instruction more impersonal.

examples.text: You **are not to leave** the school without my permission.
The European Parliament **is to introduce** a new law on safety at work.
Children **are not to be left** unsupervised in the museum.

lesson.heading: Only for events people can control

left.label: People can control it - be to + infinitive
examples: In the next few years, thousands of speed cameras **are to appear** on major roads. (or ... **will appear** ...)
The President **is to return** to Brazil later today. (or ... **will return** ...)

right.label: Nobody controls it - use will
examples: Scientists say they can't predict when or where the disease **will appear** again. (not ... the disease is to appear again)
The comet **will return** to our solar system in around 500 years. (not The comet is to return ...)

lesson.heading: Looking forward from a point in the past
lesson.text: When be to + infinitive refers to the future seen from the past, we often use it to describe what happened to someone, whether or not they could influence events.

examples.text: Matthew Flinders sailed past Tasmania in 1770, but **it was to be** a further 30 years before he landed there.
Clare Atkins **was to write** two more books about her experiences in Africa before her death in 1997.

lesson.heading: In if-clauses
lesson.text: We often use be to + infinitive in an if-clause to say that something must happen first (in the main clause) before something else can happen (in the if-clause).

examples.text: If the human race **is to survive**, we must look at environmental problems now.
The law needs to be revised if justice **is to be done**.
If Lopez **is to win** gold at the next Olympics, he needs to work on his fitness.
If Lopez **wins** gold at the next Olympics, he has said that he will retire from athletics.

lesson.text: The two if-clauses reverse cause and effect: *If Lopez is to win gold* (= the effect) *he needs to work on his fitness* (= the cause), but *If Lopez wins gold* (= the cause) *he will retire* (= the effect).

lesson.heading: be about to + infinitive
lesson.text: We use be about to + infinitive mainly in conversation to say that something will, or will not, happen in the very near future.

examples.text: **We're about to eat.** Do you want to join us?
Appearing on TV might make her famous, but **it's not about to** make her rich.
*A:* Why don't you switch it off and turn it back on again? *B:* Yes, **I was about to try** that when you came in.

exercises.prompt: Jon Stobbard has written his first new play for 15 years. Its first performance ___ at the New Victoria Theatre.
exercises.explanation: A planned, controllable event in a news report: is to be staged.

exercises.prompt: There are fears that sea levels ___ catastrophically in the next 50 years.
exercises.explanation: Rising sea levels cannot be controlled by people, so we use will, not be to.

exercises.prompt: The new safety system ___ trains automatically if they pass a danger signal.
exercises.explanation: The system acts by itself rather than by human arrangement, so will + infinitive is used.

exercises.prompt: The old design and technology programme ___ with a new computer science course.
exercises.explanation: An official arrangement, so be to + infinitive, here in the passive.

exercises.prompt: Seventy new posts ___ at the factory following a major investment by the parent company in the United States.
exercises.explanation: A controllable, planned event: are to be created.

exercises.prompt: As the temperatures fall with the onset of winter, the refugee crisis ___ more severe.
exercises.explanation: Nobody arranges this, so be to + infinitive is not possible: will become.

exercises.prompt: You need to work much harder if you ___ any chance of passing the exam.
exercises.explanation: In the if-clause, be to + infinitive gives the effect you want; the main clause gives what must happen first.

exercises.prompt: Mrs Patel is likely to become the Foreign Minister if the party ___ power at the next election.
exercises.explanation: Here the if-clause is the cause and the main clause the effect, so the present simple is used.

exercises.statement: *A:* Can you type this letter for me? *B:* Sorry, I'm just to go home. It'll have to wait until tomorrow.
exercises.explanation: Sorry, I'm just about to go home. Be about to + infinitive is used for the very near future.

exercises.statement: It started snowing an hour ago, and from the look of those clouds things are about to get a lot worse.
exercises.explanation: Correct. Be about to + infinitive is right for something happening in the very near future.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in order. The university must do something first if it wants to keep its reputation.
exercises.answer: If the university is to keep its international reputation, it must first invest in better facilities for students.
exercises.explanation: Be to + infinitive in the if-clause states the aim; the main clause states what has to happen to achieve it.

exercises.prompt: Which form does each news sentence need?

items.text: The President ___ return to Brazil later today.
The comet ___ return to our solar system in around 500 years.
Seventy new posts ___ be created at the factory.
The recent rapid rise in house prices ___ increase the demand for higher salaries.
Police officers ___ visit every home in the area.
Scientists can't predict when the disease ___ appear again.
